https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62m.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Celeste Rivas Hernandez's remains were found in September 2025 in a Tesla registered to D4vd's address By Nardine Saad ,Â Reporting from Los Angeles Â and Â Mark Savage ,Â Music correspondent Published 5 hours ago The family of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez has lobbied for the death penalty if D4vd is found guilty murdering their daughter. D4vd, who was born David Anthony Burke, is charged with killing the teenager, whose dismembered body was found in the trunk of a Tesla car registered to his address on 8 September 2025. Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges. The death penalty is under a temporary ban in California, where Burke is due to stand trial, but in a statement Hernandez' family said execution "would be perfect" if the singer was convicted of murder. In a related development, Hernandez's parents filed a civil lawsuit against Burke on Friday, seeking monetary damages including burial and funeral expenses. The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple , external US media outlets , external , makes similar claims to those raised by prosecutors in the criminal case against the singer. Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas allege that Burke caused the wrongful death, false imprisonment and childhood sexual assault of their daughter. In the court documents, they say Burke and Hernandez first met in November 2023, when she was 13 years old. Over the next 16 months, they claim, the pair would exchange almost 10,000 texts and have sex several times. "At all relevant times Burke was an adult who occupied a position of authority over decedent, a minor, and was able to and did exercise undue influence and control over her," the parents say, in papers filed last Friday. They go on to claim that Burke killed the teenager at his Hollywood Hills home, when she threatened to reveal their relationship, after allegedly sending a message that read: "I will end ur career and ur life". Figure caption, BBC reports from outside court after judge rules singer D4vd will stand trial for murder In addition to Burke, the lawsuit names several of Burke's companies and managers, his mother and a live-in security guard. Hernandez's parents allege that these people "enabled Burke to isolate" Rivas Hernandez and facilitated his travel, housing and security. Burke's management company Mogul Vision and finance manager have previously denied knowing about Burke and Rivas Hernandez, the Los Angeles Times , external reported. In July, a judge found enough probable cause for Burke to stand trial on the murder charge in the criminal case. At the time, the district attorney said he was weighing whether to seek the death penalty. In a statement on Monday, which would have been Hernandez's 16th birthday, her family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution. "If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter," read the statement, released via the family's attorney. Burke again pleaded not guilty to the charges last week and has since parted ways with his celebrity defence attorney . He is now being represented by a public defender and is due back in court on 19 October. His trial has been moved to next year. Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel has said that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence". "We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said. His office did not immediately provide comment on the civil lawsuit. Photograph: halbergman/Getty Images Los Angeles LA and San Diego residents ‘horrified’ by Trump suggesting Iran bomb them As Angelenos bemoan ‘sad situation’, those in San Diego say remark a ‘disservice’ to town with multiple naval bases Roque Planas and Sam Levin in Los Angeles Tue 6 Oct 2026 19.45 EDT First published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 18.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump’s extraordinary implication that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked condemnation across the political spectrum. As residents of the two major west coast cities awoke on Tuesday to another sweltering day in a record-breaking heatwave, the president’s comments sent blood boiling even higher. Jessica, a 28-year-old Los Angeles hair stylist, was scrolling through social media early on Tuesday morning and was shocked to see that Trump had just suggested Iran should decimate her home town. Trump suggests Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego Read more For Jessica, who declined to be identified by her full name because she fears for the safety of her Mexican-born parents, the comments marked a new low for a president who had already spent years attacking immigrant families like hers. “I was just thinking what the fuck is wrong with him?” she said while waiting for a Waymo outside grocery store in LA’s Koreatown neighborhood. “He hates us. He hates LA. He hates any Democratic state ... It’s just a really sad situation.” In southern California , Trump’s unprecedented musing before a cheering crowd at a Nebraska rally on Monday night – that perhaps a foreign power should decimate two of the country’s best-known cities – has been met with reactions ranging from deep hostility to dismissive incredulity. Gavin Newsom, the state’s governor, called the remarks “dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs”. Perhaps most of all, California residents see it as a sign of the president’s fixation on tearing down west coast progressivism and diversity, most visibly through the deployment of national guard troops in Los Angeles during a series of brutal ICE raids in 2025. During a bustling lunch service at Grand Central Market, a food hall in downtown LA, tourists and residents milled between taco stands and dumpling stalls. Many had yet to hear of the president’s threats, until asked by a reporter. One of those who had was Jens Midthun, a downtown resident who often stops at the market for coffee. View image in fullscreen Trump suggested Iran could ‘take out’ LA and San Diego at a rally. Photograph: Harry How/Getty Images “Trump has tried to paint Los Angeles as a dystopia despite it being a wonderful place,” said Midthun, sipping an iced coffee under a shaded outdoor table as the temperature approached the triple digits. (Midthun serves as the president of the downtown LA neighborhood council, but was speaking only on behalf of himself.) “It reminded me that the president is obsessed with us – obsessed with California, obsessed with Los Angeles,” Midthun said. “We try not to think about him and yet, here he is with Los Angeles’s name right there in his mouth.” Trump’s remarks have sparked a particularly strong reaction in San Diego, which is home to roughly a quarter-million veterans and has one of the largest concentrations of military personnel in the US. “His statement was so irrational, it’s hard to explain exactly what he was saying, but it sounded like he was willing to give us up,” said Gil Field, communications director for San Diego Veterans for Peace, a group that opposes the war. “It’s horrible and we’re horrified.” The military supports nearly 357,000 local jobs in the region, representing $61.3bn of San Diego county’s economy, according to a report released last year. Defense spending accounts for 22% of San Diego’s gross regional product and the area is home to multiple naval bases and Marine Corps stations, with one out of four active-duty marines based in San Diego. “This is a military town, so you’ve got bipartisan objections to his comments,” said Field, who noted that there were always concerns that San Diego could be targeted in war due to the heavy military presence. “So for him to say this about San Diego is particularly galling. He did San Diego a disservice.” Jim Desmond, a Republican naval veteran running for a congressional seat in San Diego, also offered a pointed rebuke. View image in fullscreen Navy ships are lined at the Naval Base San Diego. Photograph: The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty Images “I served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war. Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality,” Desmond said on X . “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.” Back in Los Angeles, far from the negative fantasies that Trump spins in his speeches, Midthun sees an economic powerhouse and vibrant cultural center sandwiched between the beach and the mountains, and enriched by some of the largest diaspora communities from across the world – South Korea, Mexico, El Salvador, Armenia and even Iran. “The president keeps talking about us, and talking about us,” Midthun said. “He’s got a lot of issues to solve. He should work on those issues instead of obsessing over the beautiful, great people of Los Angeles.” Explore more on these topics Los Angeles Donald Trump San Diego California West Coast US-Israel war on Iran news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.torquenews.com/1/lucid-tells.text: Related to this story Lucid Air Software Support Has No Set End Date for Bug Fixes and Security Updates Without the $950 Upgrade, Lucid Says - by Noah Washington A $10,000 Rivian Van and a $4,100 Lucid Air Expose Two Very Different Limits of EV Ownership - by Noah Washington Bolt Plans 25,000 Self-Driving Lucids for Europe, But Investors Should Watch For These 5 Signals Because That Fleet Is Larger Than Every Car Lucid Delivered in 2025 - by Armen Hareyan Lucid Air Owner Gets a $900 Lease-Return Charge for One Gouged Wheel, But Even Tesla’s 6-Inch Wear Rule Would Still Flag It - by Noah Washington Lucid Can Pull It Off, And This Is What It Probably Will Look Like With These 3 Pivot Points - by Armen Hareyan The Hyundai IONIQ 6 Gets 51 More EPA Miles on 18-Inch Wheels, Revealing a Bigger EV Design Tradeoff - by Noah Washington Screen Overkill Puts A Damper On The Otherwise Lovely 2026 Lucid Gravity Grand Touring - by Tim Healey Volvo, Volkswagen, GM and Rivian Show How OTA Updates Changed the Meaning of a Finished Car - by Noah Washington 2023 Lucid Air Touring Owner Loves His EV, but Its 2nd Rear Drive Unit Replacement in 3 Months at 30K Miles Is Pushing His Patience - by Aram Krajekian Lucid Calls Bankruptcy Report “Completely False.” One Question About AlixPartners Remains - by Noah Washington California’s New EV Subsidy Program Is Ideal For Wealthiest Buyers - by John Goreham IIHS Says Waymo Data Point to Lower Crash Rates in Limited Deployments, But NAMIC Says Insurers Still Need “Credible Claims Data” - by Noah Washington Lucid Technologies President Kay Stepper tells Torque News Bolt's 25,000 robotaxis are incremental to consumer Midsize demand. That raises the stakes on a platform already delayed into 2027 and a deal that is still nonbinding. Advertising September 23, 2026 - 6:53AM EDT By: Armen Hareyan Lucid Motors ($LCID) says the at least 25,000 autonomous vehicles Bolt wants for Europe would be built in addition to its consumer Midsize program, not taken out of it. Kay Stepper , President of Lucid Technologies and Chief Digital Officer, told Torque News that "the commercial autonomous vehicle volume is incremental to our consumer program." That one line changes the math on Lucid's broader European push . If Lucid holds to it, one delayed Midsize platform has to serve retail buyers, Bolt in Europe, and Uber in the United States. Stepper answered on the record after I emailed Lucid following my September 17 analysis of the Bolt announcement . Lucid sent the answers exclusively to Torque News on September 22, and Stepper, who leads the newly formed Lucid Technologies unit, is the named source for all of them. Who Is Bolt, the Company Behind Lucid's European Robotaxi Plan? Bolt is a ride hailing company based in Estonia that operates in more than 50 countries and 850 cities and says it serves over 200 million customers. Think of it as Europe's Uber rival, with a much smaller U.S. profile. Bolt is not just listing robotaxi rides from someone else's fleet. Its new unit, Bolt Autonomous Driving Solutions, intends to own and operate the vehicles, and Bolt wants 100,000 autonomous vehicles on its platform by 2035. Lucid is also not Bolt's only autonomy partner. Bolt has separate autonomous programs with Pony.ai and Stellantis, so Lucid is one supplier in a larger plan, not an exclusive one. Bolt CEO Markus Villig told Reuters that Europe's safety rules are significantly stricter than those in the United States and China. He also said, "Long term, we need to build this technology within the EU for EU requirements under the local standards." Does Lucid's Bolt Robotaxi Volume Come on Top of Consumer Midsize Sales? I asked, "How does Lucid get paid - vehicle sales, software/license, or both - and is there a contract value you can state on the record? Who leads the new Lucid Technologies unit, and is this fleet volume incremental to the consumer Midsize program?" Here is Stepper's full answer. "We are not sharing additional details regarding the commercial and financial terms of the partnership at this time, but the commercial autonomous vehicle volume is incremental to our consumer program. Lucid's technology platform, combined with our vehicle's space, efficiency and lower operating costs, provides a clear advantage over legacy car makers in the robotaxi market, and Lucid is ideally positioned to capitalize on this emerging opportunity." The incremental line is the news. Lucid is not planning to pull cars away from retail Midsize customers to fill Bolt's depots, which also means it needs more factory output than a retail plan alone would require. The advantage over legacy automakers is Lucid's claim, and the robotaxi market will test it. Who Pays Lucid, and Can Lucid Afford to Wait for Midsize? Lucid declined to say whether it earns money from vehicle sales, software licensing, or both, and it declined to give a contract value. That refusal matters more than it looks. Bolt owns the fleet. Unless a software or licensing stream shows up later, that makes Lucid a vehicle supplier to Bolt, paid when cars are delivered, which cannot happen before Midsize production starts. Compare that with Uber. Uber has raised its Lucid investment to $500 million alongside its vehicle commitment, while the Bolt announcement disclosed no money at all. Lucid needs that clarity. The company is majority owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, posted a second quarter net loss of more than $1 billion, and is running what it calls a $1.4 billion operational reset. Lucid ended the second quarter with $3.0 billion in total liquidity and says its runway reaches well into 2027, according to its SEC filing . Midsize production is now planned for the second half of 2027, so the runway and the launch window sit uncomfortably close together. A nonbinding 25,000 vehicle target does not fund a factory. It gives Lucid a demand story to take into its next financing conversation. Two Lucid Robotaxi Deals, Two Different Autonomy Stacks Readers keep asking whether Bolt is an extension of Lucid's Uber deal. It is not, and the difference explains what Lucid is really selling. Advertising In the United States , Uber and its fleet partners run the service, starting with the Gravity SUV Torque News has reviewed and adding Midsize later. The driving software is the Nuro Driver on Nuro's redundant sensor suite, according to Uber's investor release . That program calls for at least 35,000 vehicles. It launches in the San Francisco Bay Area this year, with Houston following in the middle of 2027. In Europe , Bolt will own the fleet itself, and the vehicles are Midsize only. The compute and sensor foundation is NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Hyperion 10, but no company has been named as the owner of the driving software. That program targets at least 25,000 vehicles under a nonbinding agreement. No city has been announced. Lucid is selling vehicles in both deals, not a single autonomy product. That is the thread connecting this deal to the Uber and Nuro alliance Torque News covered . What Is an ADS Ready Lucid Midsize, and Is It the Same Car as Cosmos? Cosmos is the first Midsize model, a crossover aimed under $50,000 as Lucid's answer to the Tesla Model Y. One of the first people to see the smaller SUV concept came away impressed, but it was supposed to launch this year and now waits for the second half of 2027. A robotaxi Midsize is not the same job as a retail Midsize. Stepper describes redundant drive by wire and a Hyperion 10 compute and sensor foundation, while the Uber version of Midsize is expected to carry the Nuro Driver. That means the Midsize platform may have to carry two different autonomy architectures plus a retail version. Lucid has not said whether the robotaxi is a Cosmos with extra hardware or a separate build, or whether it keeps a steering wheel and pedals. That is the next question Torque News is asking. Can Saudi Arabia's AMP 2 Plant Build Retail Midsize, Uber, and Bolt Cars? According to Reuters , the Bolt vehicles will come from Lucid's new Saudi facility, which is scheduled to open early next year. Lucid has said Midsize production will start first at that plant, known as AMP 2. CEO Silvio Napoli has made the delay a quality decision. "Midsize will launch only when every process and quality requirement has been met," he said on the second quarter call. Now stack the demand on that one line. Retail Cosmos buyers, a Midsize share of Uber's 35,000 vehicles, and Bolt's 25,000 all point to the same delayed platform, and Lucid has not said how AMP 2 output would be split among them. Meanwhile the Arizona side is shrinking, not growing. In June Lucid cut about 18 percent of its U.S. workforce, hourly and salaried, and eliminated the second shift at its AMP 1 factory, following the earlier cuts Torque News covered in February . Incremental demand on a delayed line after a reset is the real tension in this deal. The demand is welcome, but the capacity is still a promise. Is the Lucid and Bolt Robotaxi Deal Binding? I asked, "Is the "at least 25,000" autonomous Lucid vehicles a signed purchase agreement with volume, price, and delivery years, or a non-binding target? What is the earliest year Lucid expects to deliver the first Midsize ADS-ready vehicle to Bolt, and which city is planned first?" Here is Stepper's full answer. "What we announced was a non-binding agreement, but a clear declaration of intent as evidenced by Bolt being upfront about their planned volume. The vehicles will be built on a future Lucid Midsize vehicle, with more details regarding timing to come. The fleet rollout with Bolt will be planned city by city, based on local regulation, the readiness of authorities and the transport needs of each city. Together with Bolt, we will announce the first markets and passenger operations in the months ahead." Lucid now confirms on the record what TechCrunch reported after the announcement. The agreement is nonbinding, and Stepper frames it as "a clear declaration of intent." He gave no first delivery year and no first city. First markets and passenger operations are promised "in the months ahead," which keeps the three pivot points Torque News laid out for Lucid firmly in play. Who Owns the Level 4 Self Driving Software in Lucid's Bolt Robotaxis? Advertising I asked, "Who will own the SAE Level 4 stack that is submitted for European approval - Lucid, NVIDIA, Bolt, or another named partner? Is NVIDIA Hyperion the production compute and sensor suite, or a development reference architecture only?" Here is Stepper's full answer. "Bolt and Lucid will work together on a future Lucid vehicle platform designed to be ADS-ready for SAE Level 4 autonomous mobility. The intended architecture includes redundant, drive-by-wire capabilities and is expected to use NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Hyperion 10 as its compute and sensor foundation. Bolt's role is to integrate the vehicle, driving technology and operating infrastructure into a passenger-facing service." Lucid named the hardware. It did not name who owns the driving software that would go to European regulators, and Bolt integrates the "driving technology," in Stepper's words. That gap has real consequences. Approval, insurance, and liability all attach to someone, and right now the European program has no named company standing behind the software that drives the car. Why Level 4 Robotaxis in Europe Are Harder Than in California Europe does not have one robotaxi rulebook. The Next Web reports that the only EU wide type approval route for a fully automated car is capped at 1,500 units a year per vehicle type, and national approvals stop at each border. That is why Stepper says the rollout will go city by city. Germany passed a Level 4 framework in 2021, while other countries are still writing theirs. Competitors already have cities. Waymo announced in August that it is testing in Munich with a public service targeted for the end of 2027, and Verne and Pony.ai already run a driverless service in Zagreb booked through Uber. Bolt and Lucid have not named one city yet. How Big Is 25,000 Next to Lucid's Real Production Numbers? Lucid delivered 15,841 vehicles worldwide in 2025. It built more than that, and later restated 2025 production to 17,840 after 538 units failed an internal validation cutoff. Lucid's old 2026 guidance of 25,000 to 27,000 vehicles for its current lineup, mostly the Air and the Gravity , is no longer in effect. Lucid suspended it in May pending Napoli's review and has said it will give 2027 guidance with its year end results. The first half shows why. Lucid built 5,500 vehicles and delivered 3,093 in the first quarter after a 29 day Gravity delivery disruption, as Torque News reported in April , then built 4,774 and delivered 3,953 in the second quarter. In other words, Bolt's fleet target is larger than any full year Lucid has delivered, and Lucid currently has no official production outlook for 2026. What Should Lucid Investors Watch Next? Stepper's answers narrow the open questions. Here is what still has to show up. A named first city and a passenger launch date. A named owner of the Level 4 driving software submitted for European approval. Any step that turns the nonbinding plan into firm orders with volume, price, and years. Confirmation of whether the robotaxi Midsize is the Cosmos or a separate build. AMP 2 timing and a Midsize output split among retail, Uber, and Bolt. Whether Lucid earns software or licensing revenue from Bolt, or only vehicle sales. Torque News will keep asking Lucid and Bolt for each of these. You can follow every update in our Lucid Motors coverage . Lucid has now answered the one question that separates a fleet headline from a factory plan. Bolt's cars are supposed to be extra, on top of retail Midsize demand. Extra is the good version of this story. It only stays good if a delayed Saudi line can carry three customers, and if someone finally puts their name on the software. Does Lucid's incremental volume promise make you more confident in Midsize, or more worried about the 2027 ramp? If you were Bolt, would you wait for a named Level 4 software owner before turning 25,000 into firm orders?
